q: Entering Argostoli from the sea, you pass this buoy. On which side do you leave it?
o: On your starboard side
On either side
Close on its seaward side
why: Region A: a red can marks the port side of the channel going in.

q: You see this mark off a headland. Where is the safe water?
o: To the south of it
To the east of it
All around it
why: North cardinal: both cones point up; pass to the north of it.

q: Approaching Lefkas at night, you see a white light: six quick flashes, then one long flash. Where do you pass the mark?
o: To the north of it
To the east of it
To the west of it
why: Q(6)+LFl is a south cardinal; the long flash tells it apart from Q(3) and Q(9).

q: Your planned track passes 100 m west of this mark. Is that safe?
a: No — pass on its east side
o: Yes — west is its safe side
Yes — 100 m is enough either side
No — pass on its north side
why: East cardinal: cones base to base, light Q(3); the safe water is to the east.

q: Your pilot book says this mark guards a reef. Where is the reef?
a: To the east of the mark
o: To the west of the mark
To the north of the mark
Right underneath the mark
why: West cardinal: the safe water is to the west, so the danger lies to the east.

q: Off a point near Sivota you see this mark. How do you pass it?
a: Either side, giving it a good berth
o: Close by — it marks deep water
Leave it to port, like a lateral
Only to its north, like a cardinal
why: Isolated danger: a small danger with navigable water all round — keep well off.

q: Approaching a harbour, you find this mark ahead. What does it tell you?
o: A danger — keep well clear
The port side of the channel
A swimming area — keep out
why: Safe water mark: red and white stripes, a red ball; it often marks a fairway or landfall.

q: Off a beach near Kos you see a line of these. What are they?
o: Lateral marks — keep them to starboard
Cardinal marks — pass to their north
Safe water marks — sail between them
why: Yellow with an X: a special mark, often a bathing area limit; the chart says which.

fig.note: One of a line off the beach

q: The pilot book gives the harbour entrance light as Fl(2) R 6s. What will you see?
o: Two red flashes, each 6 seconds long
A red flash every 2 seconds
Six red flashes, then 2 s dark
why: Fl(2) = groups of two flashes; R = red; 6s = the whole cycle repeats every 6 seconds.

q: At a harbour entrance you time a white light: on for 3 seconds, off for 1, repeating. How is it shown on the chart?
o: Fl 4s — light shorter than dark
Iso 4s — light and dark equal
LFl 4s — one long flash
why: Occulting: the light is on longer than it is off; the period is 3 + 1 = 4 s.

q: Entering an unfamiliar harbour at night, you see these lights on the pierheads. Where do you steer?
a: Between them: red to port, green to starboard
o: Leave both lights on your port side
Leave both lights on your starboard side
Head for the red light, then turn
why: Region A: the red light marks the port side going in, the green the starboard side.

q: Next year you charter in the Caribbean, in IALA region B. Entering harbour from sea, on which side do you leave a red lateral mark?
o: On your port side, as in the Med
On either side — it marks a danger
On the side away from the land
why: Region B (the Americas) reverses the colours: red is left to starboard going in.

q: In a channel between two islands, you meet this mark. On which side do you leave it?
o: On your starboard side
On either side
Close on its east side
why: Lateral marks follow the direction of buoyage; heading against it, a green cone goes to port.

fig.note: Buoyage direction: north · you head south

q: At night you count nine quick white flashes, then darkness, repeating. On which side of the mark is the safe water?
o: To the east of it
To the south of it
All around it
why: Q(9) or VQ(9) is a west cardinal: think of nine o'clock on a clock face.

q: How do you pass this mark?
a: Alter to port, leaving it to starboard
o: Alter to starboard, leaving it to port
Hold course and pass close alongside
Turn back — the danger lies beyond it
why: Pass north of a north cardinal: heading east, north is to port, so the mark stays to starboard.

q: On the chart, a buoy's light is shown just as "Q" — no colour letter. What do you look for at night?
a: A white light flashing quickly, non-stop
o: A yellow light flashing quickly, non-stop
A red light flashing quickly, non-stop
A white light, one long flash every 10 s
why: No colour letter means white; Q alone is continuous quick flashing — a north cardinal.

q: Entering the channel at night, you find this light close on your starboard bow. What does it tell you?
a: You are on the wrong side — keep it to port
o: Fine — leave it to starboard as you pass
It is a starboard mark — keep it there
It is an isolated danger — pass either side
why: Going in, a red light is left to port; having it to starboard puts you outside the channel.

q: Your planned track runs between these two marks. Is it safe?
a: No — the danger lies between them
o: Yes — keep exactly halfway between
Yes — cardinals mark the channel edges
Only by day, with both marks in sight
why: A north cardinal lies north of a danger and a south cardinal south of it, so the danger is between.

q: Leaving Gouvia marina for the open sea at night, you see a flashing red light ahead, low on the water. On which side do you leave it?
o: On your port side
On either side, 50 m off
Steer straight for it
why: Heading out to sea the lateral rule reverses: red marks stay on your starboard side.

q: Coming in on the safe white sector of this light, you see it change. What does it mean?
a: You have left the safe sector — check the chart
o: You are closer — red means nearly in
The light is faulty — ignore it
The red sector is the deepest water
why: A sector light shows white over the safe approach; a coloured sector means you are off the line.
